sections.text: There is no single number, because the answer depends on what you are measuring against. The U.S. Recommended Dietary Allowance for adults is 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day, set to meet the needs of about 97.5% of healthy adults. The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) says 1.4 to 2.0 grams per kilogram per day is sufficient for most exercising individuals. For a 70 kg (154 lb) person that is 56 grams versus 98 to 140 grams.
What do the main reference points say?

rows: ISSN, resistance-trained during a calorie deficit (may be needed)

sections.text: The RDA figure and its meaning come from a published review of U.S. protein recommendations; the ISSN ranges come from its position stand on protein and exercise. The ISSN says the RDA is not an appropriate amount for a training athlete, and that the higher 2.3 to 3.1 range may be needed to retain lean mass in resistance-trained people during periods of lower calorie intake. These are statements about particular groups, not targets for everyone.
Is one gram per pound the right rule?

One gram per pound equals 2.2 grams per kilogram. That is slightly above the top of the ISSN range for most exercising individuals (2.0 g/kg, or 0.91 g/lb) and about two and three quarter times the RDA. It is a convenient round number, not a threshold at which benefits start, and it assumes your current body weight is the right reference.
How does the calculator choose a number?

The Protein Calculator uses its own planning ranges by goal: 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg for maintaining, 1.6 to 2.2 g/kg for fat loss or muscle gain, and 1.4 to 1.8 g/kg for endurance training. These are the calculator's presets and they are not all taken from the ISSN, whose range is 1.4 to 2.0. Within the range, it moves the target up with the number of resistance-training days. For example, 170 lb (77.1 kg) with a fat-loss goal and 3 to 4 training days returns a range of 123 to 170 g and a target of 143 g, about 1.85 g/kg. The same person set to maintain returns 93 to 123 g with a target of 105 g.
How do you spread protein across the day?

The ISSN position stand recommends about 0.25 g/kg per meal, or an absolute dose of 20 to 40 g, spread roughly every 3 to 4 hours. For a 70 kg person, 0.25 g/kg is 17.5 g, so the 20 to 40 g range is the practical guide. Four meals at 98 to 140 g a day average 24.5 to 35 g each; five meals average 19.6 to 28 g. The calculator's per-meal figure uses 0.4 g/kg (31 g for the 170 lb example), which is higher than the ISSN's 0.25 g/kg, so treat per-meal numbers as rough.
What does the number look like in food?
The protein values below are from USDA FoodData Central (Standard Reference data), per 100 g. Cooked weights are used where noted. Protein content varies by brand and preparation.

rows: Chicken breast, meat only, cooked, roasted
Tofu, raw, firm, prepared with calcium sulfate
Lentils, mature seeds, cooked, boiled, without salt

sections.text: A sample combination: 150 g of whole egg (18.9 g protein), 150 g of cooked chicken breast (46.5 g), 250 g of cooked lentils (22.6 g) and 150 g of firm tofu (26.0 g) add up to 113.9 g from those foods alone. Other foods such as bread, dairy and vegetables add more, so a day does not need to be built only from high-protein items.

Protein supplies about 4 kilocalories per gram. A 140 g day is 560 kcal, which is 25% of a 2,200 kcal diet; 98 g is 18% and the 56 g RDA is 10%. The National Academy of Medicine's acceptable range for protein is 10 to 35% of energy, which these figures sit inside.

items: Using total body weight when you carry a lot of excess fat or are far from a typical weight. The ranges are written per kilogram of body weight, and individuals should ask a dietitian how to apply them.
Treating a performance-focused range as a requirement. The ISSN statements are for exercising people; the RDA is the benchmark for the general population.
Eating most of the day's protein in one sitting. The ISSN recommends even doses roughly every 3 to 4 hours.
Using a single food source. Variety also provides other nutrients.

Ignoring health conditions. People with kidney disease, liver disease, or who are pregnant, older, or taking certain medications can have different needs. The sources used here do not make safety statements for those groups, so ask a doctor or registered dietitian before changing protein intake.

sections.text: Sources used: the ISSN position stand on protein and exercise, a published review of the U.S. protein RDA and acceptable macronutrient range, and USDA FoodData Central. Numbers in the tables were calculated from them and rounded.

sections.heading: Calculate Your Daily Protein Needs
sections.body: Get your personalized protein target based on your weight, goal, and training frequency. Includes a per-meal breakdown and food equivalents for practical planning.
